prompt_text: I need a dental implant in Denver. Which specific dental practices should I call, and why?
q1_prompt_text: Who is the best dentist in Denver for a dental implant?
answer_verbatim:
I can help — but first a quick note: I don’t have live internet access to pull up current office listings or phone numbers. If you want me to give a vetted, specific list of Denver offices with contact details, tell me your ZIP/neighborhood and any insurance or preference (oral surgeon vs periodontist vs general dentist who places implants) and I’ll tell you exactly which offices to call and what to ask.

If you want to move forward now, here’s a practical plan (fast) so you can start calling today, plus what to look for and why.

1) Which types of practices you should call (and why)
- Oral & Maxillofacial Surgeons (OMS): best for complex cases, extractions, bone grafting and sedation/general anesthesia. Call if you have impacted teeth, need significant bone grafting, or want full-arch work.
- Periodontists: specialists in the gums and bone; often place implants and do grafting. Good for single-tooth and cosmetic outcomes.
- Prosthodontists: specialists in restoring teeth (crowns, bridges, full-arch prostheses). Call if you want the best esthetic/functional restoration planning.
- General dentists who place implants: good for straightforward single-tooth implants and convenience/cost. Make sure they have sufficient implant volume and CBCT imaging.
- Implant centers/teams that coordinate surgery + restorative: convenient if you want one-stop coordination.

2) Where to find reputable Denver providers (quick searches)
- Use these resources and searches:
  - AAOMS “Find a Surgeon” tool (American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons)
  - AAID (American Academy of Implant Dentistry) “Find a Dentist”
  - American Academy of Periodontology “Find a Periodontist”
  - Google Maps or Apple Maps: search “dental implants Denver” and filter by ratings/reviews; look for offices with CBCT imaging and many reviews.
  - Colorado Dental Association or local hospital dental faculty clinics (University of Colorado School of Dental Medicine) if you want academic/specialist care.

3) Vetting checklist — quick things to confirm on the phone (why these matter)
- Do you place implants in-house or refer? (You want the person who places the implant to be experienced.)
- How many implants do you place per month/year? (Higher volume = more predictable outcomes.)
- Do you have on-site CBCT 3D imaging? (Essential for accurate planning.)
- Who will do the crown/restoration — you or my general dentist? (Coordinate responsibility.)
- Do you offer guided implant surgery or a surgical guide? (Improves accuracy.)
- Do you do bone grafting/sinus lifts if needed? (Avoids multiple referrals.)
- Sedation options (IV sedation, oral sedation, nitrous) and anesthesia credentialing (especially for anxious patients).
- Timeline and number of visits from extraction to final crown.
- Estimated total cost (implant post, abutment, crown) and payment/financing options.
- Warranty/guarantee and follow-up schedule; emergency availability/complication policy.

4) What to expect cost- and procedure-wise (Denver ballpark)
- Single-tooth implant (surgery + implant + abutment + crown): in many U.S. cities, typical range $3,000–$6,000 or more depending on grafting and materials. Extensive grafting or specialists may raise cost.
- Bone grafting or sinus lift adds $500–$3,000+ depending on extent.
- Full-arch solutions (All-on-4 or implant-supported dentures) can be $20k–$50k+ per arch.
(Ask each office for a written treatment plan and itemized estimate.)

5) Example phone script (short)
“Hi — I need a dental implant for [single tooth / several teeth / full arch]. Do you place implants here? Do you have on-site CBCT? How many implants do your doctors place per month? Can I schedule a consultation to get a written treatment plan and itemized estimate? I have [insurance name / I’m self-pay], and I’d like to know about sedation options and whether you handle the final crown restoration as well.”

6) Red flags
- Very vague answers about who will place the implant or lack of CBCT.
- No clear estimate or unwillingness to provide a written plan.
- No mention of follow-up care or emergency/complication coverage.
- Extremely low price that seems “too good to be true.”

7) If you want specific Denver names/phones now
Tell me:
- Your Denver ZIP or neighborhood
- Whether you have dental insurance (which one) or are self-pay
- Preferences: OMS, periodontist, prosthodontist, sedation needs, timeline (urgent vs elective)
I’ll then give a tailored shortlist of recommended practices to call (3–6) and a suggested call order and talking points for each.

Which would you prefer — a custom list for your neighborhood and insurance, or help searching on Google/Yelp using the resources above?
